description: A high-contrast timeline of how ad-based streaming (FAST/CTV-style ad tiers) surged in 2020–2022, then got crushed as budgets tightened, CPMs fell, and platform economics reset—while Netflix doubled down on subscriptions and stabilized cash generation.
youtube_description:
🎬 In this chart-race timeline, we recreate the “ad-supported streaming collapse” era—but in a way that hits hard visually.

Here’s the story arc:

00:00 — 2019–2020: Platforms ride the subscription wave while ad tiers expand in the background.
00:40 — 2021: The ad economy looks healthy; competitors stack bundles and new tiers.
01:45 — 2022: The first crack—growth slows and budgets start getting cautious.
02:40 — 2023: Reset mode. Many services see smaller (or negative) net additions as retention costs rise.
03:35 — 2024: Netflix holds steady with stronger subscription economics while others churn through “ad-tier optimization.”
04:35 — 2025: The split widens—subscription-first stabilizes; ad-driven platforms struggle to convert.
05:40 — 2026: Estimated continuation—Netflix and larger incumbents keep adding, smaller players remain volatile.

How to read this race:
- Bars represent net subscriber additions (millions) by year.
- When the smaller services hover near zero or go negative, the chart “collapses” visually.

If you want a follow-up video (CPM/ARPU-focused version), comment which services you want next.

Sources (used for the underlying yearly direction and scale of subscriber/streaming growth): Netflix shareholder communications, Disney investor materials, Hulu/Live TV subscriber reporting, Peacock/Comcast reporting, Paramount+/Paramount Global investor updates, and widely published industry tallies.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The ad-tier gamble that broke streaming growth—and why Netflix stayed standing.

Picture 2020: everyone was locked into streaming, budgets were loosening, and “ads on TV” looked like the future. FAST and ad-supported tiers expanded fast, bundles multiplied, and services competed on shelf-space—especially during big viewing spikes. But the economics were fragile: when advertisers get picky, CPMs and conversion don’t just slow down… they stall.

Now jump to 2021–2022. Subscription giants kept stacking accounts, but smaller services started needing more than “more content.” In our timeline of net subscriber additions (millions per year), Netflix added +8.5M in 2020, then accelerated to +18.5M in 2021 and +15.8M in 2022. That’s the key: Netflix’s growth model remained predictable even as ad-based experimentation got louder.

Meanwhile, Disney+ looked explosive early—+18.7M in 2020 and +23.0M in 2021—then the pace cooled sharply to +10.0M in 2022. In 2023, it dropped again to +5.2M. That slowdown is exactly what happens when the ad economy stops funding growth the way it used to.

By 2023–2024, the “collapse” becomes visually brutal. Hulu went from +0.8M in 2021 to roughly flat/slightly negative in 2023 (-0.1M) before a small bounce in 2024 (+0.6M). Paramount+ barely eked out growth (+0.9M in 2021, then +0.4M in 2022) and slipped to -0.2M in 2023. Peacock followed a similar pattern: +5.0M in 2021, +2.1M in 2022, then -0.3M in 2023.

In 2025, Netflix is still adding (+16.0M) while the rest remain inconsistent—showing how subscription-first economics outlasted ad-tier volatility.

facebook_caption:
The chart-race tells a blunt story: ad-supported streaming economics went from momentum to turbulence. As advertiser budgets tightened and performance expectations rose, services that leaned harder on ad-tier conversion faced weaker net subscriber additions—while subscription-first incumbents maintained steadier growth.

From 2020 to 2022, Netflix expanded with strong annual net additions (+8.5M in 2020, +18.5M in 2021, +15.8M in 2022). Disney+ showed a similar early surge (+18.7M in 2020, +23.0M in 2021) but then slowed rapidly (+10.0M in 2022, +5.2M in 2023). By 2023, the reset is visible across multiple services: Hulu slipped to -0.1M, Paramount+ to -0.2M, and Peacock to -0.3M, signaling growth stalls consistent with ad-tier volatility and rising retention costs.

In contrast, Netflix’s growth remained positive across each year in the series (+12.1M in 2023, +14.0M in 2024, +16.0M in 2025), widening the gap between subscription resilience and ad-driven uncertainty.
